newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish NBP ups reserves, knocks zloty to save C/A.
newsitem.headline: Polish NBP ups reserves, knocks zloty to save C/A.

text.p: The Polish central bank's decision to raise obligatory reserves on deposits and its recent interventions against the zloty are aimed to stabilise Poland's deteriorating current account, the bank's deputy head said on Tuesday.

"The unjustified rise of the zloty and problems with money supply growth for 1997, provided grounds for exchange rate and obligatory reserve moves aimed at (stabilising) the current account," Witold Kozinski told a news conference.
"Polish current account has long been deteriorating and shouldn't deteriorate any more. It is time to do something to stabilise it," he said.
On Monday, the central bank said it would raise obligatory reserves on zloty call deposits by three points to 20 percent and on currency deposits by two points to four percent, effective February 28.

Kozinski said the bank had to raise the reserves to keep its 1997 money supply growth target of 28 billion zlotys within reach after the finance ministry unexpectedly borrowed 2.2 billion zlotys from the NBP at the end of last year.
He also said the higher reserves would likely cause a rise in commercial banks' credit rates and cool down domestic demand, diminishing imports and improving the current account.

Poland's current account fell into a deficit of $984 million through November 1996 from a $4,959-billion surplus in the same period 1995. This year, it is seen rising to about $5.8 billion from an estimated $1.2 billion in 1996.
"Internal demand can be cooled in several ways, also by diminishing the liquidity of the banking system...through raising obligatory reserves," he said.

The central bank also knocked down the bullish zloty with a series of dollar- and mark-buying interventions last week, bringing it down to about 2.5 percent from the trading band centre from highs of four percent.
"Knocking the zloty down towards the central parity rate softens the zloty, works against imports and stimulates exports," Kozinski said.

He said the NBP would now wait for the market's reaction to the higher obligatory reserve requirements before deciding whether a rise in official interest rates was still needed to additionally cut credit action.

"If one raises mandatory reserves then certainly, there should not be an increase in interest rates shortly after because it may happen...that a reserve rise itself will trigger higher credit rates," Kozinski said.

The central bank has long signalled it was concerned with fast credit expansion and that it was considering raising the lombard and discount rates, now at 25 and 22 percent, respectively, or other measures, to control money supply.
